title: A Visitor for the Cellar
premise: Rafael Thornbury returns to the decaying family estate to bury his twin sister Rosalind, only to learn at the funeral that the body in the casket is not her. Three years later, still living in the house with their ailing mother and younger brother, Rafael has rationalized every sound from beneath the floorboards—until audio recordings of his own sleep reveal a second voice answering questions he never remembers asking, in Rosalind's cadence. As the 'count' approaches—a ritual date when the cellar's resident entity tallies the household and claims whoever it finds unaccounted for—Rafael uncovers that his parents bargained away one twin decades ago, and the entity has come to collect the debt. In the climax, Rafael descends to confront the thing wearing his sister's face, learning that identity itself is the currency it trades in; he offers it his memories of Rosalind to sever its claim on the family. The book ends with Rafael leading his mother and brother out at dawn, whole but hollowed—he no longer remembers his twin's face, and the recordings now capture only one voice: his own.
about_author: Astrid Nystrom is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales in rural New England, where she developed a fascination with houses that outlive their families. She writes horror about inheritance—of property, of guilt, and of names—and lives quietly in a farmhouse she refuses to describe in detail.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, present day, opening at the third anniversary of Rosalind's funeral as he replays the moment the mortician whispered that the casket held a stranger. He tends to his mother Maren's failing memory and his brother Tomas's silence. Emotional beat: grief curdling into dread—the wrongness never resolved, only buried.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV establishing the estate's strange domestic order: no doors locked, no questions after dark, mother's medication schedule like liturgy. Tomas has begun sleeping with earplugs. A cold draft rises through the kitchen floorboards though the cellar door stays padlocked. Emotional beat: the fragile normalcy Rafael has built, visibly cracking.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Hears
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Insomnia drives him to record his sleep, hoping to diagnose his nighttime wandering. Playback reveals him speaking fluently while asleep—and a second voice, dry and patient, answering questions he doesn't remember asking. The voice knows things only Rosalind knew. Emotional beat: vertigo; the rational explanations die here.

chapters.title: Tomas Counts the Stairs
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The fourteen-year-old confesses he counts footsteps overhead each night—always thirteen, always ending above his bed, though the house has twelve stairs. He shows Rafael scratches inside his closet wall spelling 'not finished.' Emotional beat: sibling alliance forming against a shared, unspeakable fear.

chapters.title: Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV searching Maren's room for answers and finding a ledger dating back forty years: payments recorded in blood type, hair, years of memory. The final entry, dated before the twins' birth, reads 'one of two, payable upon majority.' Emotional beat: horror reframed as accounting—the family was always collateral.

chapters.title: The Voice Asks Back
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He speaks aloud to the cellar for the first time, demanding answers. The voice responds through the recorder: it asks him to confirm which twin he is. When he says Rafael, it laughs softly and says, 'That's what the other one said too.' Emotional beat: identity begins to feel negotiable, unstable.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Room
chapters.summary: Maren's fragmented POV, drifting between decades. She wanders into Rosalind's preserved bedroom and speaks to it as if her daughter were alive, revealing scraps: a bargain made in desperation during poverty, a name spoken into a well, a promise that 'only one would be taken.' Emotional beat: maternal guilt surfacing through dementia like bodies through floodwater.

chapters.title: Thirteen Footsteps
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The count changes: fourteen steps now, then fifteen, each night closer to his door. He stops sleeping and witnesses the hallway mirror showing three children walking past instead of two. He tells Rafael, who finally believes him. Emotional beat: terror made concrete; the countdown has begun.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV visiting elderly neighbor Odette Vasseur, who grew up beside the Thornburys. She confirms the house has always required a tithe and warns: 'It doesn't take bodies, boy. It takes being. Whoever it keeps, everyone forgets they existed.' Emotional beat: external validation, and the first hint of an escape condition.

chapters.title: Missing Photographs
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Family albums now show gaps where Rosalind should be—faces blurred, birthdays renumbered. His own childhood photos show a single child. He realizes the entity is editing the record, preparing to erase whichever twin remains unclaimed. Emotional beat: grief for someone being deleted in real time.

chapters.title: Sleepwalking Interview
chapters.summary: Recorder transcript chapter, Rafael's POV framing it. Overnight, the second voice conducts a full interrogation of sleep-Rafael: name, birth order, what he remembers of age eighteen. Sleep-Rafael answers confidently—and incorrectly, describing events that happened to Rosalind. Emotional beat: chilling implication that his identity is already porous.

chapters.title: The Padlock Is Inside
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV breaking the cellar lock, finding not a dungeon but a perfect replica of the upstairs parlor, dusted and lived-in, set decades ago. A table set for three. On the wall, portraits: his parents, himself—and a blank frame labeled ROSALIND, waiting. Emotional beat: the horror of hospitality; something has been keeping a place for them all along.

chapters.title: Maren Confesses
chapters.summary: Alternating Maren and Rafael POV during a lucid window. Maren admits the bargain: bankrupt and pregnant with twins, she traded 'the second-born's shadow' to the thing in the well for the family's survival. It waited patiently for the twins to turn eighteen. Rosalind went down willingly to buy time. Emotional beat: devastating maternal confession; love and betrayal indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Which One Came Home
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV unraveling his own history: the funeral three years ago, the stranger in the casket, Odette's warning. He finds hospital records suggesting 'Rafael' died at birth and the surviving twin was given his name. He cannot prove he isn't Rosalind wearing a borrowed life. Emotional beat: total identity collapse at the story's midpoint hinge.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The footsteps reach his door and stop. All night, something politely knocks and asks, 'Are you complete?' Tomas answers nothing, following Odette's advice, and by dawn the knocking moves to Maren's room. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere; the rules are real and survivable but narrowing.

chapters.title: Odette's Debt
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV returning to Odette, finding her house empty except for a fresh portrait of herself on the cellar-parlor wall, aged overnight. Her car still runs in the driveway; no one remembers her but Rafael. He understands: the count collects those who know too much. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; allies are consumable.

chapters.title: Terms of Withdrawal
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV negotiating directly with the entity through the recorder. It offers terms: one resident, freely given, before the final count—or it takes the household entire. It reveals it prefers Rafael, whose self-doubt makes him 'half-claimed already.' Emotional beat: cornered pragmatism; Rafael starts planning a sacrifice that isn't himself.

chapters.title: What Rafael Decides
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV preparing Maren and Tomas to leave, forging documents, packing in daylight. But Maren refuses to go without settling the debt, and Tomas refuses to leave Rafael. Rafael secretly records a confession naming himself as the payment, intending to descend alone. Emotional beat: tragic resolve sharpening into a plan built on a lie.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV entering the cellar-parlor at midnight before the final count. The entity appears as Rosalind—then as Rafael—then as no one, cycling faces. It explains the truth: there was never a swap; both twins lived, and Rafael's doubt is the crack it entered through. Emotional beat: confrontation with the self; the monster is an argument about who he is.

chapters.title: The Offering of Memory
chapters.summary: Climax, Rafael's POV. Rather than surrendering his body or Tomas, Rafael offers the one thing the entity truly collects: his complete memory of Rosalind—every shared moment, the raw material of the identity it's been impersonating. The entity accepts, feeding on the memories until nothing remains. The blank portrait fills, then crumbles. Emotional beat: sacrificial transcendence—paying with selfhood instead of flesh.

chapters.title: One Voice
chapters.summary: Falling action, Tomas's POV. Dawn. Rafael walks out of the cellar calm and emptied, unable to say who Rosalind was or why the house matters. They drive away as the estate's windows darken one by one. The recorder plays back: a single voice, asking no questions. Emotional beat: bittersweet release; survival purchased with erasure.

chapters.title: A Visitor for the Cellar
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Rafael's POV, one year later in a new city. He is functional, loved by Tomas, haunted only by an absence he can't name. A letter arrives with no return address containing a photograph of two children—one face smudged beyond recovery—and a line in handwriting he almost recognizes: 'Thank you for the visit.' Emotional beat: quiet, unresolved dread; some debts leave receipts.
